description: Immediate, short-term and long-term physiological changes, including hypertrophy and bradycardia.
content_html:
Three Timescales of Change

Exercise affects the body across three distinct timescales, and your ability to distinguish between them is frequently tested. Immediate effects occur during the exercise session itself. Short-term effects appear in the hours following exercise, typically lasting up to 36 hours. Long-term effects emerge only after months or years of consistent training and represent genuine physiological adaptation. Mixing these up in an exam will cost marks, so developing a clear mental map of which changes belong to which category is essential.

Immediate Effects: What Happens While You Exercise

As soon as exercise begins, several changes are immediately visible or measurable. The skin becomes hot, sweaty and flushed (red): core body temperature rises as the working muscles generate heat, and the body responds by directing blood to the skin capillaries, where heat can radiate away. Sweating further cools the skin through evaporation. The increase in depth and frequency of breathing is driven by rising carbon dioxide levels in the blood: chemoreceptors detect this and signal the respiratory centre to increase breathing rate and tidal volume, delivering more oxygen and removing CO⊂2; more rapidly. Finally, heart rate rises to pump more oxygenated blood to the working muscles — this increase begins even before exercise with an anticipatory rise, driven by adrenaline release, and climbs further as exercise intensity increases.

Key Fact

The three immediate effects of exercise are: (1) hot, sweaty and red skin; (2) increased depth and frequency of breathing; (3) increased heart rate. These all begin during the exercise session and return to normal within minutes of stopping.

Short-Term Effects: The Hours After Exercise

In the period immediately after exercise and for up to 36 hours, the body experiences a range of short-term effects as it recovers. Tiredness and fatigue result from the depletion of glycogen (stored glucose) in the muscles and the accumulation of waste products. Light-headedness can occur as blood redistributes away from the brain toward the muscles during exercise, or when exercise stops suddenly and blood pools in the lower limbs before circulation fully adjusts. Nausea may follow high-intensity efforts, particularly in the stomach, as blood flow to the digestive system is significantly reduced during exercise. Aching, cramp and most importantly DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) develop as the micro-damage to muscle fibres — especially after eccentric contractions or unfamiliar movements — triggers an inflammatory response that peaks 24–48 hours post-exercise.

DOMS is caused by micro-tears in the muscle fibres, particularly following eccentric (lengthening) contractions — for example, lowering a weight under control, running downhill or landing from a jump. These micro-tears are repaired by the body, and during that repair process the muscle fibres are rebuilt slightly thicker and stronger than before. This is the fundamental mechanism of muscle hypertrophy. Experienced athletes experience less DOMS because their muscles have already adapted to a given level of stress. When DOMS does appear, it is typically a signal that a new training stimulus has been applied and adaptation is underway — but the soreness itself should not be severe enough to limit movement significantly.

Long-Term Effects: Adaptations From Months of Training

Consistent exercise over months and years causes permanent physiological adaptations in multiple body systems. These long-term effects represent the body becoming structurally and functionally more efficient at the demands placed on it.

Body shape may change: regular resistance training increases muscle size and reduces relative body fat, while prolonged endurance training may produce a leaner physique with visible muscular definition. Specific components of fitness improve: muscular endurance, speed, suppleness, muscular strength, cardiovascular endurance and stamina all increase with appropriately designed training programmes. For example, a sprinter who trains over many months will improve their speed and explosive strength; a cross-country runner will develop greater cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance in their legs.

Two of the most significant long-term cardiovascular adaptations are cardiac hypertrophy and bradycardia. Cardiac hypertrophy refers to the heart growing larger and stronger as a muscle in response to the repeated demands of training. A larger, stronger heart can pump more blood per beat — a greater stroke volume. Because stroke volume is higher, the heart does not need to beat as many times per minute to deliver the same cardiac output. This produces bradycardia: a lowered resting heart rate. While the average untrained person has a resting heart rate of around 60–80 beats per minute, elite endurance athletes such as cyclists or distance runners may have resting heart rates of 35–50 bpm. Mo Farah, for example, is reported to have had a resting heart rate in the low 40s during the peak of his marathon career.

Key Fact

The chain: regular training → cardiac hypertrophy (the heart grows larger) → greater stroke volume per beat → bradycardia (lower resting heart rate needed to maintain cardiac output). These are all long-term adaptations — they take months or years of consistent training to develop.

Hypertrophy as a general term refers to the growth in size of a muscle caused by an increase in the size of individual muscle fibres. When applied to skeletal muscles (e.g. the biceps or quadriceps group), it is the result of progressive resistance training: repeated eccentric and concentric contractions under load cause micro-tears, which repair larger and stronger over time. When the term is used specifically as “cardiac hypertrophy,” it refers to the same growth process applied to the heart muscle itself, driven by the sustained cardiovascular demands of endurance training. In both cases, the underlying stimulus is the same — the body adapts to repeated stress by growing the muscle tissue — but the practical outcomes differ: skeletal muscle hypertrophy increases strength and power for movement, while cardiac hypertrophy increases stroke volume and reduces resting heart rate.
exam_tip_html: The most common error on questions about effects of exercise is confusing the three timescales. A short-term effect such as DOMS appears hours to days after exercise — it is not the same as the immediate effects (hot skin, increased heart rate) that occur during exercise. In “describe” and “explain” questions, always state the timescale explicitly: “in the long term, after months of training, the heart undergoes hypertrophy, which leads to bradycardia.” For 6-mark “analyse” questions, go beyond listing: connect the adaptation to a named component of fitness and then to a sporting performance benefit. For example: “Cardiac hypertrophy increases stroke volume, improving cardiovascular endurance, which allows a club cyclist to sustain a higher pace over a 40 km time trial without fatigue.”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Immediate effects (during exercise) include hot/sweaty/red skin, increased breathing rate and depth, and increased heart rate — these reverse within minutes of stopping.
  • Short-term effects (up to 36 hours after) include fatigue, light-headedness, nausea, and DOMS — caused by glycogen depletion, lactic acid, and micro-tears in muscle fibres.
  • Long-term effects (months to years of training) include improved fitness components, cardiac hypertrophy and, as a result, bradycardia — a permanently lower resting heart rate due to greater stroke volume.

practice_questions.text: Identify one immediate effect of exercise on the body.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: increased heart rate; increased breathing rate/depth; hot, sweaty or red skin. Accept equivalent physiological descriptions.

practice_questions.text: State two short-term effects of exercise that may appear within 36 hours of a training session.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct short-term effects from: tiredness/fatigue; light-headedness; nausea; aching muscles; DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness); cramp. Do not accept 'increased heart rate' (immediate effect). Award once for the same point expressed differently.

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the resting heart rates of three athletes before and after a 6-month endurance training programme.

Athlete | Resting HR before (bpm) | Resting HR after (bpm)
Alex   | 74                      | 61
Beth   | 68                      | 55
Carlos | 72                      | 58

Calculate the mean reduction in resting heart rate across all three athletes. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly calculating each individual reduction (Alex: 13 bpm; Beth: 13 bpm; Carlos: 14 bpm); 1 mark for summing correctly (13 + 13 + 14 = 40 bpm) and dividing by 3; 1 mark for the correct final answer: 13.3 bpm (accept 13 or 13.3). Units required (bpm) for the final answer mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain how cardiac hypertrophy leads to bradycardia in a trained endurance athlete.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining cardiac hypertrophy as the long-term increase in the size of the heart muscle due to training; 1 mark for explaining that this means the heart can pump a greater stroke volume per beat; 1 mark for explaining that a higher stroke volume means the heart beats fewer times to deliver the same cardiac output; 1 mark for naming or defining bradycardia as a lower resting heart rate (below normal, typically below 60 bpm in trained athletes). Full marks require the logical chain to be clear.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old county-level basketball player has been following a structured fitness programme for eight months. Analyse the long-term physiological effects this programme is likely to have had on her body, and how these effects might improve her performance on court.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Detailed, well-developed response identifying multiple long-term effects (cardiac hypertrophy, bradycardia, muscular hypertrophy, improved muscular endurance/strength/speed, possible changes to body composition). Each adaptation is linked to a mechanism (e.g. cardiac hypertrophy increases stroke volume, lowering resting HR) and then to a specific basketball performance benefit (e.g. sustained cardiovascular output across four quarters; greater explosive power for jumping). Technically accurate language used throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): Most key long-term effects identified with generally accurate explanations. At least one adaptation linked to a basketball context. May lack development on mechanisms.

Developing (2 marks): One or two long-term effects mentioned but not fully explained. Limited sporting application to basketball.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic correct point about a long-term effect (e.g. the heart gets bigger) with little or no explanation or sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A club runner claims that feeling sore the day after a hard run means she has overtrained and should rest completely. Evaluate whether this claim is accurate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Clear identification of DOMS and its mechanism (micro-tears in muscle fibres, especially from eccentric contractions). Explains that DOMS is a normal, expected short-term effect rather than a sign of overtraining. Discusses when DOMS is benign (manageable soreness, peaks 24-48 hours) vs when it signals overtraining (severe, persistent, affecting movement). Considers both sides: complete rest is not always necessary — light activity, massage or ice baths can manage DOMS while allowing recovery; but if soreness is extreme or persistent, rest is warranted. Justified conclusion reached.

Secure (3-4 marks): DOMS explained correctly; the claim is challenged with some justification. Some appreciation of both sides (DOMS is normal; severe cases need rest). Sporting context present.

Developing (2 marks): DOMS mentioned but not well explained. Limited evaluation — may agree or disagree with the statement without full justification.

Emerging (1 mark): Identifies DOMS or muscle soreness as the relevant concept but provides little analysis.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a LONG-TERM effect of regular endurance training?
What is the correct definition of cardiac hypertrophy?
options: A lower resting heart rate caused by training
The long-term increase in the size of the heart muscle through training
An immediate rise in heart rate at the start of exercise
The thickening of artery walls due to high blood pressure

knowledge_checks.q: DOMS stands for delayed onset muscle _____, which typically peaks 24-48 hours after exercise.
An anticipatory rise in heart rate before exercise begins is triggered by the release of _____.
Match each effect of exercise to the correct timescale:

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three immediate effects of exercise on the body.
flashcard_questions.a: Hot/sweaty/red skin; increased breathing rate and depth; increased heart rate.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an anticipatory rise in heart rate?
flashcard_questions.a: A rise in heart rate before exercise begins, triggered by adrenaline release.
Micro-tears in muscle fibres, especially from eccentric contractions, triggering inflammation.

flashcard_questions.q: When does DOMS typically peak after exercise?

flashcard_questions.a: The long-term increase in the size of the heart muscle caused by regular training.
A lower than normal resting heart rate, typically below 60 bpm, caused by long-term training.

flashcard_questions.q: Explain the link: cardiac hypertrophy → bradycardia.
flashcard_questions.a: Bigger heart pumps greater stroke volume per beat, so fewer beats needed per minute.
The increase in size of individual muscle fibres caused by progressive resistance training.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two long-term effects of endurance training on the cardiovascular system.
flashcard_questions.a: Cardiac hypertrophy and bradycardia (lower resting heart rate).

flashcard_questions.q: Why does skin become red and flushed during exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Blood is redirected to skin capillaries to radiate heat and cool the body.

flashcard_questions.q: State two short-term effects of exercise that appear within 36 hours after training.
flashcard_questions.a: DOMS and fatigue/tiredness. (Also accept: nausea, light-headedness, cramp.)

flashcard_questions.q: Name three components of fitness that improve as a long-term effect of regular exercise.
flashcard_questions.a: Any three of: muscular endurance, speed, suppleness, muscular strength, cardiovascular endurance.

glossary_terms.definition: The rise in heart rate that occurs before the start of exercise, triggered by adrenaline release and anticipation of physical effort.
Delayed onset muscle soreness; muscle pain and stiffness that typically peaks 24-48 hours after unfamiliar or high-intensity exercise, caused by micro-tears in the muscle fibres.
The long-term increase in the size and muscle mass of the heart resulting from regular, sustained exercise training.
A lower than normal resting heart rate, typically below 60 bpm, caused by the heart becoming more efficient through long-term training.
The increase in the size of individual muscle fibres as a result of resistance training, producing greater muscle bulk and strength.
The volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle with each heartbeat; regular training increases stroke volume, allowing the heart to pump more blood per beat.
